Unlinked files that remain open are visible through the open-file table, which is exactly what `lsof` exposes.

**Why it works:** Each open descriptor in `/proc/<PID>/fd` carries the path of the file it points at, and unlinked entries are tagged `(deleted)` in the `lsof` output.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `stat` needs a live pathname
- `find` cannot enumerate inodes that no longer have a directory entry
- `diff` compares file contents and is unrelated to open descriptors

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, manage files and directories on a Linux system.
questions.question:
Two team members have edited a shared `nginx.conf` over the weekend and want to review the changes side by side in a single terminal window so they can reconcile them line by line. The pair would like the differences highlighted in two columns rather than the default unified output.

Which utility is best suited to this side-by-side review?

choices.text: `sdiff nginx.conf.old nginx.conf.new`
choices.explanation: `sdiff` prints both files in two columns separated by a gutter that marks added, removed, and changed lines, which is the side-by-side view requested.

choices.text: `diff -q nginx.conf.old nginx.conf.new`
choices.explanation: `-q` reports only whether the files differ without showing any content, so it cannot support a line-by-line review.

choices.text: `cp nginx.conf.old nginx.conf.new`
choices.explanation: `cp` overwrites one file with the other instead of producing a comparison; the changes would be lost.

choices.text: `stat nginx.conf.old nginx.conf.new`
choices.explanation: `stat` reports inode metadata such as size and timestamps but does not compare file contents.

questions.tip: Pick the utility whose default output is a two-column layout.
questions.explanation:
The correct option is the side-by-side comparison tool.

**Why it works:** `sdiff` prints corresponding lines from the two files in adjacent columns with markers showing which side the change came from.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `diff -q` produces only a binary same-or-different verdict
- `cp` overwrites rather than compares
- `stat` reports metadata, not contents

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, manage files and directories on a Linux system.
questions.question:
The storage team needs a pointer that always resolves to the current release directory under `/opt/app/releases/2026-06-12/`, so that scripts can reference `/opt/app/current` regardless of which release is live. The target may live on a different filesystem from the link, and the link must survive deletion and recreation of the target.

Which command creates the correct pointer?

choices.text: `ln -s /opt/app/releases/2026-06-12 /opt/app/current`
choices.explanation: A symbolic link stores the target path as a string, can cross filesystem boundaries, and can be relinked without touching the data.

choices.text: `ln /opt/app/releases/2026-06-12 /opt/app/current`
choices.explanation: A hard link requires the source and target to share an inode on the same filesystem and cannot reference a directory on standard Linux filesystems.

choices.text: `cp -r /opt/app/releases/2026-06-12 /opt/app/current`
choices.explanation: `cp -r` duplicates the data rather than creating a pointer, so the two trees would diverge as the release directory changes.

choices.text: `mv /opt/app/releases/2026-06-12 /opt/app/current`
choices.explanation: `mv` renames the original directory, which removes the release path that other tools may still reference.

questions.tip: Only one type of link can span filesystems and point at a directory.
questions.explanation:
A symbolic link is the only Linux link type that can target a directory and cross filesystem boundaries.

**Why it works:** `ln -s` records the target path as a string, so the link continues to resolve correctly after the target is replaced and is independent of the underlying filesystem.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Hard links to directories are not permitted and cannot cross filesystems
- Copying duplicates data instead of pointing to it
- Moving renames the source and breaks anything else that referenced it

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, manage files and directories on a Linux system.
questions.question:
While auditing `/dev`, a junior engineer lists entries and sees `/dev/sda` shown with a leading `b` in the permissions column and `/dev/ttyS0` shown with a leading `c`. The senior engineer asks them to explain what the two prefixes mean in terms of how data is transferred to and from each device.

Which description correctly differentiates the two device types?

choices.text: Block devices transfer data in fixed-size, randomly addressable blocks, while character devices stream data one byte at a time in sequence.
choices.explanation: This matches the kernel's distinction: block devices such as disks support random access in block units while character devices such as serial lines deliver a byte stream.

choices.text: Block devices are always read-only mount points, while character devices are writable raw partitions.
choices.explanation: Block devices are routinely writable and writability is independent of being block or character type.

choices.text: Block devices represent network interfaces, while character devices represent storage media.
choices.explanation: Network interfaces are not present in `/dev` as block devices; storage media is typically block-addressable, not character.

choices.text: Block devices are software pseudo-devices, while character devices map to physical hardware.
choices.explanation: Both categories include real hardware and pseudo-devices; the difference is the access pattern, not the backing.

questions.tip: Think about how the kernel addresses each device when reading or writing.
questions.explanation:
The leading letter in `ls -l` of a `/dev` node tells you whether the kernel treats the device as block or character.

**Why it works:** `b` denotes block-addressable storage that supports random access in fixed-size blocks, and `c` denotes a stream-oriented character device delivered one byte at a time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Read-only is unrelated to device class
- Storage is block, not character
- Both classes can be hardware or pseudo-devices

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, manage files and directories on a Linux system.
questions.question:
Following a deployment, the build engineer needs to materialise a new empty configuration file at `/etc/myapp/feature.conf` and confirm its inode number for an audit log. The path's parent directory already exists and the engineer wants to perform both steps with single-purpose tools.

Which TWO commands complete the task?

choices.text: `touch /etc/myapp/feature.conf`
choices.explanation: `touch` creates the empty file when it does not exist and updates timestamps if it does.

choices.text: `stat /etc/myapp/feature.conf`
choices.explanation: `stat` prints inode number, size, ownership, and timestamp metadata for the newly created file.

choices.text: `mkdir /etc/myapp/feature.conf`
choices.explanation: `mkdir` would create a directory of that name, not an empty regular file.

choices.text: `file /etc/myapp/feature.conf`
choices.explanation: `file` reports content type rather than the inode number requested for the audit log.

choices.text: `ln -s /dev/null /etc/myapp/feature.conf`
choices.explanation: Symlinking to `/dev/null` produces a link, not an empty regular file, and writes would be discarded.

questions.tip: Match each step to its single-purpose utility.
questions.explanation:
Creating an empty file is the canonical role of `touch`, and the audit metadata is produced by the `stat` utility.

**Why it works:** `touch` creates a zero-byte file if the path does not exist, and `stat` prints inode metadata including the inode number for the audit log.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `mkdir` produces a directory
- `file` reports content type, not inode metadata
- A symlink to `/dev/null` is a link, not an empty file

skills: 2.1: Given a scenario, manage files and directories on a Linux system.
questions.question: Match each filesystem utility to the task it most directly performs.

choices.text: Prints the absolute path of the current working directory
choices.explanation: It outputs the shell's current directory as an absolute path.

choices.text: Identifies the content type of a file by inspecting its bytes
choices.explanation: It reads magic numbers and metadata to classify the file's contents.

choices.text: Removes a directory only when it is empty
choices.explanation: It refuses to delete non-empty directories, providing a safety check.

choices.text: Queries a prebuilt index to find paths matching a name quickly
choices.explanation: It searches a periodically refreshed database rather than walking the filesystem live.

questions.tip: Pair each utility with the single task it is purpose-built for.
questions.explanation: Each utility has a narrow, well-defined role: reporting the current directory, identifying file type from contents, safely removing empty directories, and looking up paths in an index.

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
The platform team is provisioning a new analyst named Sara. They want her home directory created automatically with the skeleton files copied in, her default shell set to `/bin/bash`, and her primary group set to a newly created `analysts` group. The group already exists on the host.

Which command satisfies all three requirements?

choices.text: `useradd -m -s /bin/bash -g analysts sara`
choices.explanation: `-m` creates the home directory and seeds it from `/etc/skel`, `-s` sets the login shell, and `-g` sets the primary group to an existing group.

choices.text: `useradd -M -s /bin/bash -G analysts sara`
choices.explanation: `-M` suppresses creation of the home directory, and `-G` adds the user to a supplementary group rather than setting the primary group.

choices.text: `adduser --no-create-home --shell /bin/bash --gid analysts sara`
choices.explanation: `--no-create-home` defeats the requirement to create the home directory with skeleton files.

choices.text: `usermod -m -s /bin/bash -g analysts sara`
choices.explanation: `usermod` modifies an existing account; it cannot create one, so the command fails because the user does not yet exist.

questions.tip: Distinguish primary group from supplementary group flags carefully.
questions.explanation:
The correct invocation creates the user with a home directory, sets the shell, and assigns the existing group as the primary group.

**Why it works:** Lowercase `-g` selects the primary group and `-m` triggers home creation seeded from `/etc/skel`.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `-M` skips the home directory
- `--no-create-home` does the same
- `usermod` cannot create a missing account

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
Following a compliance review, the security team must immediately prevent the `contractor1` account from logging in with a password without removing the account or deleting any files it owns. The account must remain present in `/etc/passwd` for audit reasons and must be reactivatable later by an administrator.

Which command achieves this lock?

choices.text: `passwd -l contractor1`
choices.explanation: `passwd -l` prefixes the encrypted password in `/etc/shadow` with an exclamation point, blocking password authentication without removing the account.

choices.text: `userdel contractor1`
choices.explanation: `userdel` removes the account from `/etc/passwd`, which violates the audit requirement.

choices.text: `chage -d 0 contractor1`
choices.explanation: Forcing password expiry still permits login once a new password is set and does not prevent authentication.

choices.text: `chsh -s /sbin/nologin contractor1`
choices.explanation: Changing the shell stops interactive logins but does not lock the password, and protocols that do not spawn a shell could still authenticate.

questions.tip: The requirement is to block password authentication while preserving the account record.
questions.explanation:
Locking via `passwd -l` invalidates the stored hash while leaving the account intact.

**Why it works:** Prefixing the hash with `!` makes it impossible to match any submitted password, while the account row remains in `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow`.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `userdel` deletes the record entirely
- forcing expiry only nags for a new password
- changing the shell does not lock the password

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
A security control requires that every interactive user's password expire 90 days after it was last changed, and that the user be warned 7 days before expiry. The administrator wants to apply the policy to the `jdoe` account without altering any other expiration values.

Which command sets the maximum age and warning period correctly?

choices.text: `chage -M 90 -W 7 jdoe`
choices.explanation: `-M` sets the maximum number of days a password is valid, and `-W` sets the number of days warning before expiry.

choices.text: `chage -m 90 -W 7 jdoe`
choices.explanation: Lowercase `-m` is the minimum age between password changes, which would prevent the user from changing their password for 90 days.

choices.text: `usermod -e 90 jdoe`
choices.explanation: `usermod -e` sets an absolute account expiry date as days since epoch, not a recurring password lifetime.

choices.text: `passwd -x 90 -w 7 jdoe`
choices.explanation: While `passwd` can edit ageing fields on some distributions, the long-running cross-distribution tool for this policy is `chage`, and the flags here mix utilities.

questions.tip: Distinguish maximum age from minimum age carefully.
questions.explanation:
Password ageing fields in `/etc/shadow` are managed through `chage`.

**Why it works:** Uppercase `-M` controls the maximum days before forced change, and `-W` sets the days of warning before expiry.

**Why the others don't work:**
- lowercase `-m` is the minimum age
- `usermod -e` is an absolute expiry date
- the `passwd` flag combination is non-portable

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
After a recent audit, the operations lead asks for the UID, primary GID, and every supplementary group of the currently logged-in account so the entries can be pasted into a ticket. The command must work without needing a username argument and must show the numeric IDs along with the names.

Which command produces this information?

choices.text: `id`
choices.explanation: Run with no arguments, `id` prints the calling user's UID, GID, and supplementary groups in numeric and name form.

choices.text: `whoami`
choices.explanation: `whoami` prints only the effective username, with no UID or group data.

choices.text: `who`
choices.explanation: `who` lists logged-in sessions including login terminals but does not report UID or supplementary groups.

choices.text: `last`
choices.explanation: `last` reads `/var/log/wtmp` and shows login history rather than current account attributes.

questions.tip: Pick the utility whose default output is the current identity in numeric and symbolic form.
questions.explanation:
`id` is the single command that prints UID, primary GID, and supplementary groups for the caller.

**Why it works:** With no argument it operates on the invoking process's credentials and prints both numeric and symbolic forms.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `whoami` returns only the username
- `who` enumerates sessions
- `last` shows historical logins

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
While reviewing `/etc/passwd`, a new administrator sees that the `postgres` account has a UID of 116 and a shell of `/usr/sbin/nologin`, while their own account `alice` has UID 1001 and shell `/bin/bash`. They ask why the postgres entry is treated differently from a normal user account.

Which statement BEST explains the categorisation?

choices.text: It is a service account whose low UID falls within the system range, so it is intended for running a daemon rather than interactive login.
choices.explanation: System and service accounts conventionally occupy UIDs below the regular user range and disable login by setting a `nologin` shell.

choices.text: It is a guest account that automatically expires after the first login because it has a UID below 1000.
choices.explanation: There is no automatic guest expiry tied to UID; service accounts are persistent.

choices.text: It is an interactive user account that has been temporarily disabled by setting `nologin` as a shell.
choices.explanation: Service accounts ship with `nologin` by design rather than as a temporary lockout, and a UID of 116 is outside the normal interactive range.

choices.text: It is a placeholder created by `groupadd` so the daemon can share a GID with future users.
choices.explanation: `groupadd` creates a group, not a user entry in `/etc/passwd`.

questions.tip: Look at both the UID range and the assigned shell to classify the account.
questions.explanation:
The `postgres` entry is a service account, characterised by its low UID and `nologin` shell.

**Why it works:** Distributions reserve UIDs below the regular-user threshold for system and service accounts that own files and run daemons; setting the shell to `nologin` prevents interactive logins.

**Why the others don't work:**
- there is no automatic guest expiry
- `nologin` here is by design, not a temporary lockout
- `groupadd` does not create user entries

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
The standardisation team wants every newly created user on a build host to inherit a custom `.bashrc` and a preconfigured `~/.config/myapp/` directory at account creation, without modifying existing accounts. The change must be transparent to anyone running `useradd -m` later.

Which TWO actions accomplish this?

choices.text: Place the customised `.bashrc` in `/etc/skel/.bashrc`.
choices.explanation: Files in `/etc/skel` are copied into new home directories when `useradd -m` is invoked.

choices.text: Create `/etc/skel/.config/myapp/` with the desired default contents.
choices.explanation: Subdirectories under `/etc/skel` are recursively copied to new home directories on account creation.

choices.text: Edit `/etc/profile` to source the user's custom dotfiles globally.
choices.explanation: `/etc/profile` affects all sessions globally and does not seed per-user dotfiles into home directories.

choices.text: Run `usermod -m` against every future user immediately after creation.
choices.explanation: `usermod -m` relocates an existing home directory and does not seed new dotfiles.

choices.text: Add the files to `/etc/passwd` as an extended GECOS field.
choices.explanation: `/etc/passwd` stores account metadata, not user-profile templates.

questions.tip: Identify the directory whose contents are copied verbatim into each new home directory.
questions.explanation:
The skeleton directory `/etc/skel` is copied into each newly created home, so placing both the dotfile and the directory tree there is sufficient.

**Why it works:** When `useradd -m` is invoked, the contents of `/etc/skel` are recursively copied into the new home directory, preserving subdirectory structure.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `/etc/profile` runs globally but does not populate home directories
- `usermod -m` moves an existing home, not templating
- `/etc/passwd` has no GECOS provision for files

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment.
questions.question: Match each account database file to the information it stores.

choices.text: Username, UID, primary GID, home directory, and login shell for each account
choices.explanation: It is the world-readable account index used during login lookups.

choices.text: Encrypted password hashes and password-ageing fields, readable only by root
choices.explanation: Protected hashes and the ageing controls live here to keep them off world-readable files.

choices.text: Group names, GIDs, and membership lists for supplementary groups
choices.explanation: This file defines groups and which users are extra members of each one.

choices.text: Template files copied into a newly created user's home directory
choices.explanation: Its contents seed home directories when an account is created with home creation enabled.

questions.tip: Think about which file each piece of account data is stored in by design.
questions.explanation: Linux splits account data across several files so that secret material can be readable only by root while non-sensitive entries remain world-readable for lookups.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
After editing the Nginx configuration, an administrator wants the running master process to reread its config without terminating any existing client connections. The change should propagate to worker processes through the normal configuration reload mechanism.

Which signal should be sent to the master PID?

choices.text: `SIGHUP` (signal 1)
choices.explanation: Many long-running daemons including Nginx interpret `SIGHUP` as a request to reload configuration without dropping connections.

choices.text: `SIGKILL` (signal 9)
choices.explanation: `SIGKILL` immediately terminates the master and severs every client connection.

choices.text: `SIGTERM` (signal 15)
choices.explanation: `SIGTERM` initiates a graceful shutdown rather than a configuration reload.

choices.text: `SIGSTOP` (signal 19)
choices.explanation: `SIGSTOP` suspends the process; the configuration is not reread and clients stall.

questions.tip: Match the standard reload convention for daemons.
questions.explanation:
`SIGHUP` is the conventional reload signal for daemons.

**Why it works:** Nginx's master handler for `SIGHUP` reparses the configuration and spawns new workers while existing workers finish in-flight requests.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `SIGKILL` is unmaskable termination
- `SIGTERM` requests shutdown
- `SIGSTOP` suspends execution

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
During an interactive `ssh` session, an engineer launches a long-running data import that should keep running after they log out, with output redirected to a log file. They also want the import to start in the background immediately and survive the shell exiting cleanly.

Which invocation meets all of these constraints?

choices.text: `nohup ./import.sh > import.log 2>&1 &`
choices.explanation: `nohup` makes the process ignore `SIGHUP`, the redirection captures output, and `&` runs the command in the background.

choices.text: `./import.sh > import.log 2>&1 &`
choices.explanation: Without `nohup`, the process receives `SIGHUP` when the controlling terminal closes and is likely to exit.

choices.text: `exec ./import.sh > import.log 2>&1`
choices.explanation: `exec` replaces the shell with the import, which still terminates when the SSH session ends.

choices.text: `bg ./import.sh > import.log 2>&1`
choices.explanation: `bg` resumes an already-stopped job; it cannot be used to start a fresh command directly.

questions.tip: Combine three requirements: HUP immunity, redirection, and background placement.
questions.explanation:
All three constraints are satisfied by wrapping the command in `nohup`, redirecting output, and appending `&`.

**Why it works:** `nohup` arranges for `SIGHUP` to be ignored when the terminal closes, the redirection keeps stdout and stderr safe, and `&` puts the job in the background immediately.

**Why the others don't work:**
- omitting `nohup` exposes the process to `SIGHUP`
- `exec` replaces the shell but the parent SSH still terminates
- `bg` resumes existing jobs and cannot start one

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
A daily report generator at PID 4421 is consuming most of one CPU core and causing latency in user-facing services. The administrator wants to lower its scheduling priority without restarting it, so that interactive processes preempt it more easily.

Which command applies the change?

choices.text: `renice +10 -p 4421`
choices.explanation: `renice` changes the niceness of an existing process; a more positive value makes it less favoured by the scheduler.
`nice` launches a new command at a chosen niceness; it cannot retarget an already-running PID and a negative value would increase priority.

choices.text: `kill -CONT 4421`
choices.explanation: `SIGCONT` resumes a stopped process and does not change scheduling priority.

choices.text: `pkill -USR1 4421`
choices.explanation: `pkill` matches process names rather than PIDs and `SIGUSR1` is application-defined, not a niceness control.

questions.tip: Pick the utility purpose-built for adjusting an existing process's niceness.
questions.explanation:
Niceness on an existing PID is changed with `renice`.

**Why it works:** A positive niceness value lowers the scheduling priority, and `-p` targets a specific PID.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `nice` only sets niceness for a freshly launched command
- `SIGCONT` resumes stopped processes
- `pkill` plus `SIGUSR1` does not adjust priority

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
While troubleshooting a sluggish host, an engineer runs `ps` and notices several entries marked with state `Z` whose parent process is still alive. They want to understand what these entries actually represent so they can decide whether intervention is required.

Which description correctly characterises a process in this state?

choices.text: A terminated child whose exit status has not yet been reaped by its parent, occupying only a process table entry.
choices.explanation: A zombie has finished executing but its parent has not called `wait`, so the kernel retains the slot for the exit code.

choices.text: A process that is currently consuming CPU time in user mode and cannot be preempted.
choices.explanation: An actively running process is shown with state `R`, not `Z`.

choices.text: A process that is blocked waiting on disk I/O and will resume once the syscall completes.
choices.explanation: Uninterruptible disk-wait shows as state `D`, not `Z`.

choices.text: A process that has been suspended by `SIGSTOP` and is waiting for `SIGCONT`.
choices.explanation: Stopped processes appear with state `T`, distinct from zombie.

questions.tip: Tie the state letter to its lifecycle role.
questions.explanation:
State `Z` denotes a zombie process.

**Why it works:** A zombie is the leftover process-table entry of a terminated child whose parent has not yet collected the exit status with `wait`.

**Why the others don't work:**
- running maps to `R`
- uninterruptible sleep maps to `D`
- stopped maps to `T`

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
A backup script must run at 02:30 every day except weekends, with stdout and stderr emailed to the operator. The administrator has been granted permission to create entries in the user crontab and wants the simplest schedule expression that captures Monday through Friday at the chosen time.

Which crontab line accomplishes this?

choices.text: `30 2 * * 1-5 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh`
choices.explanation: The five fields encode minute 30, hour 2, any day-of-month, any month, and day-of-week 1 through 5, which is Monday to Friday.

choices.text: `2 30 * * 1-5 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh`
choices.explanation: Swapping minute and hour fires the job at 02:02 on minute 30 of an hour-of-day-30, which is invalid and would never run.

choices.text: `30 2 * * 0,6 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh`
choices.explanation: Day-of-week 0 and 6 are Sunday and Saturday, the inverse of the requested schedule.

choices.text: `@daily /usr/local/bin/backup.sh`
choices.explanation: `@daily` runs every day at midnight without distinguishing weekends.

questions.tip: Remember the cron field order: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week.
questions.explanation:
The cron expression directly captures the requested schedule.

**Why it works:** Minute 30, hour 2, with the day-of-week range 1 to 5, runs at 02:30 on weekdays only.

**Why the others don't work:**
- swapped minute and hour produces an impossible field value
- 0 and 6 select weekends instead of weekdays
- `@daily` ignores weekends

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
While a foreground compile is occupying the terminal, an engineer needs to stop the build temporarily, list any jobs the shell is tracking, and then resume it in the background so the prompt is freed up. The compile must continue from where it was paused rather than restarting.

Which TWO actions complete the workflow?

choices.text: Press Ctrl+Z to suspend the foreground job.
choices.explanation: Ctrl+Z sends `SIGTSTP`, stopping the foreground job and returning the shell prompt.

choices.text: Run `bg %1` to resume the stopped job in the background.
choices.explanation: `bg` resumes a stopped job by sending `SIGCONT`, leaving the prompt free.

choices.text: Press Ctrl+C to interrupt the foreground job.
choices.explanation: Ctrl+C sends `SIGINT`, which typically terminates the build rather than pausing it.

choices.text: Run `fg %1` to resume the job.
choices.explanation: `fg` resumes the job in the foreground, which does not free the prompt.

choices.text: Run `kill -9 %1` to background the job.
choices.explanation: `SIGKILL` terminates the job immediately and cannot resume execution.

questions.tip: Think about which keystroke pauses and which command resumes in the background.
questions.explanation:
Suspending with Ctrl+Z then resuming with `bg` is the canonical pattern for moving a foreground job to the background.

**Why it works:** `SIGTSTP` stops the job without killing it, after which `bg` issues `SIGCONT` to let it continue while detached from the terminal.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Ctrl+C interrupts rather than pauses
- `fg` returns the job to the foreground
- `SIGKILL` terminates

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment.
questions.question: Match each process-inspection tool to its most distinctive capability.

choices.text: Traces system calls and signals between a process and the kernel
choices.explanation: It attaches to a process and prints each syscall as it is invoked.

choices.text: Displays the process hierarchy as a tree of parent-child relationships
choices.explanation: It visualises PPID-to-PID nesting starting from init or systemd.

choices.text: Reports per-process CPU, memory, and I/O statistics over time
choices.explanation: It is part of the sysstat suite and samples per-PID resource usage.

choices.text: Lists open files, sockets, and devices held by processes
choices.explanation: It enumerates each process's open file descriptors and the paths they point to.

questions.tip: Each utility has a distinct angle of process visibility.
questions.explanation: Each tool inspects a different dimension of process behaviour: syscalls, hierarchy, resource time series, and open descriptors.

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
After adding a third-party repository to a Rocky Linux host, the administrator wants to install one of its packages while making sure that subsequent automatic updates never replace the distribution's stock `httpd` package with the third-party rebuild. The exclusion must remain in effect for every future `dnf update`.

Which configuration change satisfies the requirement?

choices.text: Add `exclude=httpd` to the third-party repository's `.repo` file under `/etc/yum.repos.d/`.
choices.explanation: Setting `exclude=` inside the specific repository file scopes the exclusion to that source, leaving the base repository free to update `httpd`.

choices.text: Run `dnf remove httpd` after each update to clear the third-party copy.
choices.explanation: This is reactive, removes the package outright, and does not actually prevent reinstallation on the next run.

choices.text: Disable GPG verification for the third-party repository so its `httpd` is rejected.
choices.explanation: Disabling signature checks weakens security and does not block the package from installing.

choices.text: Add `enabled=0` to the base OS repository so its packages no longer update.
choices.explanation: Disabling the base repository would prevent every system package from receiving security updates.

questions.tip: Scope the exclusion to the repository that should not provide the package.
questions.explanation:
Pinning the exclusion inside the third-party repository file is the targeted fix.

**Why it works:** `exclude=` inside a specific `.repo` file applies only when that repository is consulted, so the base repository continues to deliver updates for `httpd`.

**Why the others don't work:**
- removing after the fact is reactive
- disabling GPG weakens trust without affecting selection
- disabling the base repo blocks all OS updates

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
While onboarding a new Ubuntu host, the administrator adds a vendor-supplied APT repository. They must ensure that packages from that repository are verified against a key the vendor publishes, and that an unsigned or mismatched package is rejected even if its dependencies resolve correctly.

Which step provides that guarantee?

choices.text: Import the vendor's GPG public key into APT's trusted keyring so signatures on the repository's metadata can be verified.
choices.explanation: APT validates the `Release` file signature against trusted keys, and any package whose hash does not chain back to that signed manifest is refused.

choices.text: Add the repository line to `/etc/apt/sources.list` with the `[trusted=yes]` option.
choices.explanation: `trusted=yes` instructs APT to skip signature verification, which is the opposite of the requirement.

choices.text: Run `apt-get install --allow-unauthenticated` whenever pulling from that repository.
choices.explanation: This flag explicitly bypasses verification rather than enforcing it.

choices.text: Enable `apt-transport-https` and rely on TLS to authenticate packages.
choices.explanation: Transport encryption protects fetch integrity but does not verify the publisher's signature on the package content.

questions.tip: Authenticity of the publisher comes from a cryptographic signature, not from transport.
questions.explanation:
Trusting the vendor's GPG key is what lets APT verify the signed metadata chain.

**Why it works:** The signed `Release` file lists per-package hashes; any package that does not match the signed manifest fails verification and is rejected.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `[trusted=yes]` disables verification
- `--allow-unauthenticated` bypasses it
- HTTPS protects transit, not publisher identity

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
A development team needs to install a Python library called `requests` into a project virtual environment so it does not affect the system Python installation. The host's distribution package manager also offers a `requests` package, but it is older than the version the project needs.

Which approach satisfies the team's requirement?

choices.text: Activate the project's virtual environment and run `pip install requests` inside it.
choices.explanation: `pip` installed inside an activated virtual environment places packages under the venv's site-packages directory, isolating them from system Python.

choices.text: Install the distribution package globally and override it with `pip install --user requests`.
choices.explanation: `--user` writes to the user's profile, still affecting every Python invoked under that account and possibly conflicting with the distribution copy.

choices.text: Use `cargo install requests` since it provides language-agnostic package isolation.
choices.explanation: `cargo` is the Rust package manager and does not install Python libraries.

choices.text: Use `npm install requests` and add the project to `PYTHONPATH`.
choices.explanation: `npm` manages Node.js modules and cannot deliver a Python library to the Python interpreter.

questions.tip: Match the language ecosystem with its own package manager.
questions.explanation:
Inside an activated venv, `pip install` places the library under the venv's path, isolating it.

**Why it works:** Activation prepends the venv's `bin` and adjusts `PYTHONPATH` so installed packages live alongside that interpreter only.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `--user` is global to the account
- `cargo` is for Rust
- `npm` is for Node.js

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
A host has both `vim-tiny` and `vim` installed, and three different scripts invoke `editor` expecting their preferred binary. The administrator wants `editor` to resolve to `/usr/bin/vim.basic` by default and to remember that choice across reboots, using the standard Debian mechanism for selecting alternative implementations.

Which command performs this configuration?

choices.text: `update-alternatives --set editor /usr/bin/vim.basic`
choices.explanation: `update-alternatives --set` pins the symlink for the `editor` link group to the specified path, persisting across upgrades.

choices.text: `ln -sf /usr/bin/vim.basic /usr/bin/editor`
choices.explanation: Manually replacing the symlink bypasses the alternatives database, and the next package upgrade will overwrite the link.

choices.text: `export EDITOR=/usr/bin/vim.basic` in `/etc/profile`
choices.explanation: This sets a shell environment variable but does not change the system-wide `editor` symlink that scripts call directly.

choices.text: `apt-get install --reinstall vim` to make it the default.
choices.explanation: Reinstalling refreshes the package but does not change the alternatives selection.

questions.tip: Use the framework that distributions provide for swapping default implementations.
questions.explanation:
Debian-family distributions provide a database of alternative implementations managed by `update-alternatives`.

**Why it works:** `--set` records the user's manual choice and updates the master symlink, and the choice persists across package updates.

**Why the others don't work:**
- a manual symlink is clobbered on upgrade
- `EDITOR` is shell-level only
- reinstalling does not flip the alternative

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
The infrastructure team is standing up an internal time source for a fleet of Linux servers that must keep their clocks accurate within tens of milliseconds. The service should listen on UDP port 123 and use the chrony implementation that ships with the distribution.

Which service is being configured?

choices.text: NTP (Network Time Protocol) for clock synchronisation over UDP/123.
choices.explanation: `chrony` is an NTP implementation that uses UDP port 123 to exchange time samples with peers and clients.

choices.text: DHCP for dynamic host configuration over UDP/67-68.
choices.explanation: DHCP allocates network configuration to clients and uses ports 67 and 68.

choices.text: DNS for hostname resolution over UDP/53.
choices.explanation: DNS resolves names to IP addresses on port 53 and does not provide time synchronisation.

choices.text: SMTP for mail submission over TCP/25.
choices.explanation: SMTP delivers email and operates over TCP, not UDP/123.

questions.tip: Map the well-known port number to the protocol it serves.
questions.explanation:
Time synchronisation on UDP/123 is the Network Time Protocol.

**Why it works:** `chrony` is a modern NTP daemon that listens on UDP/123 and disciplines the local clock against upstream sources.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DHCP is for address allocation
- DNS is for name resolution
- SMTP is for mail

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment.
questions.question:
After enabling a vendor APT repository, the deployment team wants to make sure that the next `apt-get update` and `apt-get upgrade` cycle authenticates packages from the new repository correctly and only installs packages that pass verification. The vendor publishes its key as an armored file and has provided a list of supported distribution codenames.

Which TWO actions are required?

choices.text: Import the vendor's GPG public key into `/etc/apt/keyrings/` and reference it from the repository's `signed-by` option.
choices.explanation: Modern APT scopes verification to the keyring referenced by `signed-by`, so the key is only trusted for that repository.

choices.text: Add the repository definition under `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/` with the correct distribution suite.
choices.explanation: APT only consults the repository if a properly formatted source entry exists with the matching codename.

choices.text: Set `APT::Get::AllowUnauthenticated true;` in `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99vendor`.
choices.explanation: This globally bypasses verification, defeating the security requirement.

choices.text: Disable the distribution's official keyring before installing the vendor package.
choices.explanation: Removing the distro keyring breaks authentication for every other repository.

choices.text: Run `apt-key add -` to drop the vendor key into the global trusted keyring.
choices.explanation: `apt-key` is deprecated and gives the key authority over every repository, which is overly broad.

questions.tip: Pair a properly scoped key with a properly scoped repository definition.
questions.explanation:
The supported pattern places the vendor's key in a per-repository keyring and ties it to the source entry via `signed-by`.

**Why it works:** APT verifies the signed `Release` file using only the keyring named in `signed-by`, so trust is scoped to that vendor and other repositories are unaffected.

**Why the others don't work:**
- allowing unauthenticated breaks the guarantee
- disabling the distro keyring breaks all updates
- legacy `apt-key add` is deprecated and overly broad

skills: 2.4: Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment.
questions.question: Match each service to the primary function it provides on a Linux host.

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, manage Linux using systemd.
questions.question:
After hand-editing `/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service` to change the `ExecStart` line, the administrator notices that `systemctl restart myapp` still launches the binary with the old arguments. They have confirmed the file on disk contains the new value and the syntax is valid.

Which step is required before restarting the service?

choices.text: Run `systemctl daemon-reload` to reload the systemd manager configuration.
choices.explanation: `daemon-reload` re-parses unit files from disk so subsequent restart commands act on the updated definition.

choices.text: Run `systemctl unmask myapp` to clear a hidden masking state.
choices.explanation: `unmask` only matters if the unit was previously masked, which is not implied here.

choices.text: Reboot the host to clear the cached unit definitions.
choices.explanation: Rebooting works as a side effect but is unnecessary; `daemon-reload` is the supported path.

choices.text: Re-enable the service with `systemctl enable --now myapp`.
choices.explanation: Enabling links the unit into a target for boot, not into the running manager's in-memory copy.

questions.tip: Edits on disk are not visible to systemd until its in-memory state is refreshed.
questions.explanation:
Systemd keeps a parsed copy of every unit in memory; updates on disk require an explicit reload.

**Why it works:** `daemon-reload` discards the cached unit definitions and reparses them so the next `restart` picks up the new `ExecStart`.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `unmask` is unrelated unless the unit was masked
- rebooting is heavy-handed
- `enable` writes symlinks for boot, not in-memory state

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, manage Linux using systemd.
questions.question:
A baseline policy requires that the legacy `telnet.socket` unit can never be started, even accidentally by a dependency or a future package install. Simply disabling the unit leaves it possible to start with `systemctl start` on demand, which is not acceptable.

Which command enforces the policy?

choices.text: `systemctl mask telnet.socket`
choices.explanation: `mask` symlinks the unit to `/dev/null`, preventing it from being started either manually or by dependency activation.

choices.text: `systemctl disable telnet.socket`
choices.explanation: `disable` only removes boot-time activation; the unit can still be started manually or pulled in by another unit.

choices.text: `systemctl stop telnet.socket`
choices.explanation: `stop` halts the running instance but does not prevent future starts.

choices.text: `systemctl reset-failed telnet.socket`
choices.explanation: `reset-failed` clears the failed state counter and has no effect on whether the unit can be started.

questions.tip: Find the action that makes a unit impossible to start, not merely disabled at boot.
questions.explanation:
Masking is the strict form of disabling.

**Why it works:** `systemctl mask` links the unit name to `/dev/null` so any start attempt resolves to a no-op unit and is refused.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `disable` allows manual or dependency start
- `stop` only handles the current instance
- `reset-failed` is a counter reset

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, manage Linux using systemd.
questions.question:
Following a slow boot, the operations engineer wants a per-unit breakdown of which units contributed most to the startup time, sorted from slowest to fastest. They want to use the standard systemd diagnostic utility rather than parsing journals manually.

Which command produces that breakdown?

choices.text: `systemd-analyze blame`
choices.explanation: `systemd-analyze blame` lists every unit's initialisation time, sorted descending, exposing the biggest contributors to boot delay.

choices.text: `systemctl list-units --failed`
choices.explanation: This lists units in failed state and reveals nothing about boot duration.

choices.text: `journalctl -b -p err`
choices.explanation: Filtering the journal for errors highlights failures but does not produce timing per unit.

choices.text: `hostnamectl status`
choices.explanation: `hostnamectl status` reports hostname and OS metadata, not startup timing.

questions.tip: Look for the analyser whose subcommand attributes elapsed time to each unit.
questions.explanation:
`systemd-analyze blame` is the canonical command for per-unit boot timing.

**Why it works:** It reads boot statistics recorded by systemd and prints each unit with its initialisation duration, sorted slowest first.

**Why the others don't work:**
- failed-unit listings ignore timing
- error journals show failures
- `hostnamectl` reports identity metadata

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, manage Linux using systemd.
questions.question:
The platform team wants a periodic task that copies a database dump to off-host storage every six hours, with management lifecycle, logging, and isolation handled by systemd rather than cron. The task itself runs a script and needs to survive reboots so it fires at predictable intervals.

Which systemd unit pair best implements this?

choices.text: A `.service` unit that invokes the script and a `.timer` unit that activates the service every six hours.
choices.explanation: Systemd timers replace cron entries by activating a paired service unit on a schedule, with logging via the journal and standard unit management.

choices.text: A `.target` unit that pulls in the script through dependencies.
choices.explanation: Targets group units for state transitions; they do not provide scheduling.

choices.text: A `.mount` unit that runs the script before mounting the export.
choices.explanation: Mount units describe filesystem mount points and do not run scheduled jobs.

choices.text: A single `.service` unit with `RestartSec=21600` to fire every six hours.
choices.explanation: `RestartSec` controls retry delay on restart, not periodic scheduling.

questions.tip: Scheduling under systemd uses one unit type to fire and another to do the work.
questions.explanation:
Periodic execution under systemd is achieved by pairing a timer with a service.

**Why it works:** The `.timer` triggers the matching `.service` on the configured interval, with all output captured by the journal.

**Why the others don't work:**
- targets group units, not schedule them
- mounts attach filesystems
- `RestartSec` is for restart back-off, not interval scheduling

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, manage Linux using systemd.
questions.question:
An administrator needs to set the host's static hostname to `web01.example.com`, and they want the change to update `/etc/hostname` and notify the kernel without requiring a reboot. The standard systemd utility for this purpose must be used.

Which command applies the change?

choices.text: `hostnamectl set-hostname web01.example.com`
choices.explanation: `hostnamectl set-hostname` updates the static hostname, syncs the runtime hostname, and writes `/etc/hostname`.

choices.text: `sysctl kernel.hostname=web01.example.com`
choices.explanation: This sets only the runtime value and does not persist across reboots in `/etc/hostname`.

choices.text: Edit `/etc/hosts` to map 127.0.1.1 to the new hostname.
choices.explanation: `/etc/hosts` provides a name resolution mapping but does not change the system hostname.

choices.text: `resolvectl status` to refresh the hostname database.
choices.explanation: `resolvectl status` reports the DNS resolver state and does not configure the hostname.

questions.tip: Pick the systemd-aware utility designed for identity configuration.
questions.explanation:
`hostnamectl set-hostname` is the supported systemd interface for hostname changes.

**Why it works:** It writes the static hostname to `/etc/hostname`, updates the kernel's runtime hostname, and notifies subscribed services through D-Bus.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `sysctl` updates only the kernel runtime value
- `/etc/hosts` is a resolver file
- `resolvectl` manages DNS state

skills: 2.5: Given a scenario, manage Linux using systemd.
questions.question:
A new application service has been packaged with a unit file at `/lib/systemd/system/dataproc.service`. The administrator wants it to start automatically on every boot and to be running immediately, without performing two separate steps and a manual `start` afterwards.

Which TWO outcomes does `systemctl enable --now dataproc.service` produce?

choices.text: It creates the symlinks that cause the unit to be pulled in by the default target at boot.
choices.explanation: `enable` creates the symlinks under `multi-user.target.wants/` or the relevant `WantedBy` target.

choices.text: It starts the unit immediately in the current boot.
choices.explanation: The `--now` flag combines `enable` with `start` so the unit transitions to active immediately.

choices.text: It masks the unit to prevent later disabling.
choices.explanation: Enabling is the opposite of masking and does not lock the unit against disabling.

choices.text: It rewrites the unit file with the current runtime configuration.
choices.explanation: `enable` does not edit the unit file; only `edit` modifies the contents through drop-ins.

choices.text: It schedules a one-shot timer for the unit at the next reboot.
choices.explanation: No timer is created; boot activation comes from the standard target symlinks.

questions.tip: Decompose the combined flag into its two effects.
questions.explanation:
The combined `enable --now` form arranges for boot-time activation and immediate start.

**Why it works:** `enable` writes the symlink graph the manager uses at boot, while `--now` synchronously runs `start` on the unit so it is active right away.

**Why the others don't work:**
- masking is the inverse action
- the unit file content is unchanged
- no timer unit is created

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server.
questions.question:
An engineer needs to run a stock `nginx:1.27` image so that the container's port 80 is reachable on the host at port 8080, the container detaches from the terminal, and it is named `web` for easy reference. Other containers on the same Docker network must still be able to reach the service through its container name.

Which command meets all of these constraints?

choices.text: `docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27`
choices.explanation: `-d` detaches, `--name web` assigns a discoverable name, and `-p 8080:80` maps host port 8080 to container port 80.

choices.text: `docker run -it --name web -p 80:8080 nginx:1.27`
choices.explanation: `-it` is foreground/interactive and the port mapping is reversed, exposing host port 80 to container port 8080.

choices.text: `docker run -d --network host nginx:1.27`
choices.explanation: `--network host` skips port mapping entirely and is unrelated to choosing host port 8080.

choices.text: `docker run --rm -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27`
choices.explanation: `--rm` runs interactively and removes the container on exit; no name is set and the container does not detach.

questions.tip: Check detach, name, and port-mapping direction together.
questions.explanation:
The detached, named container with the correct port mapping is the right invocation.

**Why it works:** `-d` releases the terminal, `--name web` lets other containers resolve it by name on a user-defined network, and `-p 8080:80` publishes the host-to-container port mapping.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `-it` keeps it foreground and the mapping is reversed
- `--network host` bypasses port mapping
- `--rm` does not detach and assigns no name

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server.
questions.question:
While hardening a Dockerfile for a Node.js application, a developer wants the resulting image to run its process as a non-root account, and they want the `node` binary to be the entrypoint with command-line arguments overridable at run time. The image base is `node:20-alpine`.

Which Dockerfile snippet matches the requirement?

choices.text: Use `USER node` plus `ENTRYPOINT ["node"]` and `CMD ["server.js"]`.
choices.explanation: `USER` drops privileges to a non-root account, `ENTRYPOINT` fixes the executable, and `CMD` supplies default arguments that the caller can override.

choices.text: Use `USER root` plus `ENTRYPOINT ["server.js"]`.
choices.explanation: Running as `root` defeats the hardening goal, and the entrypoint must invoke an interpreter for a script.

choices.text: Use `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` with no `USER` or `ENTRYPOINT` line.
choices.explanation: Without `USER`, the container runs as root; the prompt explicitly requires non-root execution.

choices.text: Use `FROM node:20-alpine AS final` and rely on the base image's default user.
choices.explanation: The official Node Alpine image does not run as a non-root user by default; the `node` user must be selected explicitly.

questions.tip: Combine privilege drop, fixed executable, and overridable arguments.
questions.explanation:
The correct snippet drops privileges and uses the canonical `ENTRYPOINT` plus `CMD` pattern.

**Why it works:** `USER node` runs the process under an unprivileged account; `ENTRYPOINT` fixes the executable while `CMD` supplies overridable default arguments at run time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- staying as `root` violates the requirement
- omitting `USER` leaves the process privileged
- the base image does not switch user automatically

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server.
questions.question:
After a long development sprint the build host has accumulated dozens of dangling images and stopped containers that no project still references. The administrator wants to reclaim space by removing only those artefacts, leaving named volumes, networks in active use, and tagged images intact.

Which command performs that cleanup?

choices.text: `docker system prune`
choices.explanation: `system prune` removes stopped containers, dangling images, and unused networks but, without `-a`, preserves tagged images, and without `--volumes`, preserves named volumes.

choices.text: `docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq)`
choices.explanation: This force-removes every container including running ones and does nothing about dangling images.

choices.text: `docker volume prune`
choices.explanation: Volume prune removes unused volumes, but the requirement explicitly keeps volumes intact and also asks for image cleanup.

choices.text: `docker rmi $(docker images -q)`
choices.explanation: This deletes every image regardless of whether it is tagged or referenced, exceeding the requested scope.

questions.tip: Pick the prune scope that matches exactly what should be deleted.
questions.explanation:
`docker system prune` is the scoped cleanup that matches the requirement.

**Why it works:** Without extra flags it removes stopped containers, dangling images, and unused networks while preserving named volumes and tagged images.

**Why the others don't work:**
- force-removing containers does not handle dangling images
- volume prune removes the wrong category
- removing all images is too broad

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server.
questions.question:
A monitoring agent must be deployed in a container that needs each instance to obtain a unique IP address directly on the physical LAN, behaving as if it were a separate host on the same broadcast domain. Bridge networking with port mapping has been ruled out by the network team.

Which container network driver should be selected?

choices.text: `macvlan`, which assigns a unique MAC and IP on the parent interface's LAN.
choices.explanation: macvlan exposes each container as a first-class layer-2 endpoint on the host's network, with its own MAC and IP.

choices.text: `host`, which shares the host's network namespace with the container.
choices.explanation: Host networking removes isolation rather than providing a distinct LAN endpoint per container.

choices.text: `none`, which gives the container no network at all.
choices.explanation: `none` disables networking and prevents the agent from reaching anything.

choices.text: `overlay`, which creates a multi-host virtual network on top of UDP.
choices.explanation: Overlay is for cross-host service mesh networking, not direct LAN attachment.

questions.tip: Choose the driver that places each container directly on the physical LAN.
questions.explanation:
`macvlan` is the driver that meets the requirement.

**Why it works:** It attaches each container as a distinct layer-2 endpoint on the parent interface's network, giving it its own MAC and IP and allowing direct LAN reachability.

**Why the others don't work:**
- host networking is shared not separate
- none disables networking
- overlay is a multi-host virtual network

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server.
questions.question:
Following a deploy failure, an engineer needs to stream the most recent log output from a container named `api` and continue watching new entries as they arrive. The logs should come from the container engine's logging driver, not from an in-container log file.

Which command produces this stream?

choices.text: `docker logs -f api`
choices.explanation: `docker logs` retrieves output the engine captured from the container's stdout and stderr, and `-f` follows new entries.

choices.text: `docker exec api tail -f /var/log/app.log`
choices.explanation: This reads a file inside the container, not the engine's captured log stream.

choices.text: `docker inspect api --format '{{.LogPath}}'`
choices.explanation: `inspect` reports the path to the log file but does not stream its contents.

choices.text: `docker stats api`
choices.explanation: `docker stats` shows resource usage metrics, not log output.

questions.tip: Use the subcommand designed to expose captured stdout and stderr.
questions.explanation:
`docker logs -f` is the right command.

**Why it works:** The engine captures stdout and stderr from PID 1 inside the container, and `-f` continues to tail those streams as new lines are written.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `exec tail` reads an in-container file
- `inspect` reports metadata
- `stats` shows resource usage

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server.
questions.question:
A PostgreSQL container must persist its data so the database survives container deletion and recreation, and the storage must be managed by the engine rather than a bind mount under `/var/lib/`. The team prefers a named volume that can be referenced by other containers without specifying a host path.

Which TWO commands accomplish the setup?

choices.text: `docker volume create pgdata`
choices.explanation: Creates a named volume managed by the engine that other containers can mount by name.

choices.text: `docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16`
choices.explanation: Mounts the named volume at the database's data directory so contents persist beyond the container's lifecycle.

choices.text: `docker run -d -v /tmp/pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16`
choices.explanation: This is a bind mount from a host path, not an engine-managed named volume.

choices.text: `docker run --tmpfs /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16`
choices.explanation: `--tmpfs` stores data in memory and is wiped on container stop.

choices.text: `docker cp ./pgdata postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data`
choices.explanation: `docker cp` copies files into a running container's filesystem and does not provide persistence.

questions.tip: Pair volume creation with the mount that references it by name.
questions.explanation:
Creating a named volume and mounting it into the container's data directory persists state across the container's lifecycle.

**Why it works:** The engine manages the named volume on a known host path under its data root, and the volume reference inside `-v` resolves by name rather than absolute path.

**Why the others don't work:**
- bind mounts use host paths
- tmpfs is in memory
- `docker cp` does not persist

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server.

choices.text: Build the image with `docker build` and assign it a tag
choices.explanation: Building turns the Dockerfile into a tagged image stored locally.

choices.text: Run the image as a container with `docker run`, exposing any required ports
choices.explanation: Running creates a container instance from the built image and starts the workload.

choices.text: Inspect the running container with `docker logs` or `docker exec` to verify it started correctly
